record.narrative: There are no existing claims, so I am registering a first-wave set of mechanistic, binary-marker hypotheses. Direction coding is set so that a positive reported estimate supports the hypothesized mechanistic contrast: direction -1 means the exposed group is expected to have a more negative dependency score, i.e. stronger dependency, whereas direction +1 means the exposed group is expected to have a less negative dependency score, i.e. weaker dependency. I restricted initial comparisons to predictors with ample exposed and comparator sample sizes, so the 20-per-cell discovery requirement should be met. The main set tests: (1) oncogene addiction for KRAS, BRAF, EGFR, and ERBB2; (2) NRF2 stress dependence induced by KEAP1 loss; (3) p53-axis dependence, predicting that TP53 loss weakens MDM2 and USP7 dependencies; (4) SWI/SNF paralog compensation, predicting that SMARCA4 or ARID1A loss increases SMARCA2 dependency; (5) MYC amplification associated with transcriptional, translational, and helicase dependencies (POLR2A, RPL11, DHX9); (6) MSI-associated WRN synthetic lethality; (7) RB1 loss associated with mitotic chromosome-segregation dependency KIF18A; (8) KRAS-mutant signaling dependence on STAT3; and (9) less certain but plausible secretory-trafficking hypotheses linking EGFR amplification to RIT1 and ERBB2 amplification to TMED10. These are association hypotheses in the supplied lung cell-line CRISPR dataset; they do not imply causality or generalizability beyond this dataset. All proposals are initialized as unresolved pending empirical effect sizes and uncertainty estimates.

For the first analysis wave I selected 12 registered claims that cover the major mechanistic axes in the registered set and have enough exposed and comparator observations for stable Welch comparisons. The batch includes canonical oncogene-dependency hypotheses (KRAS, BRAF, EGFR, ERBB2), KEAP1 loss associated with NRF2 stress dependence, p53-axis loss associated with weaker MDM2 and USP7 dependencies, SWI/SNF paralog-compensation hypotheses for SMARCA2, a MYC-amplification/transcription-dependency hypothesis, MSI-high WRN synthetic-lethality-like association, and RB1-loss KIF18A mitotic dependency. I deferred RPL11/DHX9 MYC hypotheses, KRAS-STAT3 cross-talk, and the more speculative EGFR-RIT1 and ERBB2-TMED10 hypotheses until the first-wave results can guide follow-up allocation. No new claims are registered at this stage because the existing registered claims are sufficient for the initial discovery screen. All estimates will be interpreted as signed to the pre-specified hypothesis direction; positive values indicate evidence supporting the mechanistic direction, with importance judged against the 10% relative-difference clinical significance threshold and the reported uncertainty.

I interpreted all signed estimates relative to the pre-registered hypothesis direction: a positive signed estimate supports the registered hypothesis, and a negative signed estimate opposes it. To judge the 10% clinical threshold, I used the absolute overall mean of each dependency outcome as the baseline scale, so approximately: KRAS threshold ≈0.0245, BRAF ≈0.0248, EGFR ≈0.0250, ERBB2 ≈0.0260, NFE2L2 ≈0.0093, MDM2 ≈0.0269, SMARCA2 ≈0.0415, POLR2A ≈0.0255, USP7 ≈0.0093, WRN ≈0.0301, KIF18A ≈0.0256. H1 has a positive signed estimate of 0.0137 (about 5.6%), below threshold, but its interval reaches the threshold, so the overall KRAS effect is unresolved and deserves subgroup follow-up. H2 is negative/opposite and not clinically meaningful, so the overall BRAF mutation hypothesis is rejected. H3 is exactly borderline for significance (0.0252, about 10.1%), with a 95% interval spanning nearly zero, so it is scientifically interesting but statistically and multiplicity-fragile; I keep it unresolved and propose adenocarcinoma follow-up. H4 is null-like and rejected. H5 strongly opposes the registered direction: after reversing direction, KEAP1 loss is associated with a much less negative NFE2L2 dependency score by about 0.796, far above the outcome-specific 10% threshold; I reject the original hypothesis but register the opposite-direction claim as an accepted in-dataset discovery and propose a batch-interaction audit because a very large effect could be technical or context dependent. H6 has small positive support for TP53 loss weakening MDM2 dependency, but the interval includes zero and only reaches threshold at the upper end, so it is unresolved and I propose a lineage-subtype refinement. H7 is a strong accepted effect: SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, well beyond threshold with a very tight positive interval. H8 is small, opposite to hypothesis, and not clinically meaningful, so the overall ARID1A-loss hypothesis is rejected. H9 is far below threshold and rejected. H12 is a very strong accepted effect: TP53 loss is associated with much weaker USP7 dependency, about 0.802 on the signed direction, far above threshold; however this is surprising and potentially dataset- or context-dependent, so I request one independent validation for H12. H13 is strongly accepted: MSI-high is associated with much stronger WRN dependency, about 0.790, consistent with synthetic-lethality-like behavior, and I propose adenocarcinoma follow-up. H14 is small and not meaningful, so the RB1-loss KIF18A hypothesis is rejected. All conclusions are associations in this supplied dataset and do not establish causality or generalizability without validation.

The independent validation for H12 confirms the discovery result. H12 is signed in the positive direction, so a positive estimate means that TP53-loss cells have a less negative USP7 dependency score, i.e. weaker USP7 dependency. The discovery estimate was +0.802 with a 95% Welch interval of approximately +0.782 to +0.822, and the independent validation estimate is +0.797 with a multiplicity-aware independent interval of approximately +0.769 to +0.824. The magnitude is far above the 10% clinical-significance threshold using the overall USP7 mean scale, and the independent interval remains entirely positive and large. Therefore I accept the overall H12 association: in this dataset, TP53 loss is strongly associated with weaker USP7 dependency. I close investigation of the original overall comparison because the claim is now supported by both discovery and independent validation, although related subtype/interaction refinements can remain separate. The broader interim conclusion is: (1) supported associations include SMARCA4 loss -> stronger SMARCA2 dependency, MSI-high -> stronger WRN dependency, KEAP1 loss -> weaker NFE2L2 dependency, and TP53 loss -> weaker USP7 dependency with validation; (2) negative overall findings include BRAF mutation -> stronger BRAF dependency, ERBB2 amplification -> stronger ERBB2 dependency, ARID1A loss -> stronger SMARCA2 dependency, MYC amplification -> stronger POLR2A dependency, RB1 loss -> stronger KIF18A dependency, and the originally registered KEAP1 loss -> stronger NFE2L2 dependency, which was reversed; (3) unresolved overall findings include KRAS mutation vs KRAS dependency, EGFR amplification vs EGFR dependency, and TP53 loss vs MDM2 dependency, plus several deferred MYC/oncogene cross-talk hypotheses; (4) no causal claim is warranted, and external generalizability remains uncertain. The most informative next analyses are to test the registered adenocarcinoma subgroup refinements for KRAS, EGFR, MDM2, WRN, and USP7; to run the SMARCA4-by-ARID1A interaction and KEAP1-by-batch audits; and then to prioritize independent validation of the strongest unvalidated accepted claims, especially KEAP1 loss -> weaker NFE2L2 dependency because the effect is large and directionally surprising, followed by SMARCA4 -> SMARCA2 and MSI-high -> WRN.

These proposals follow up the strongest accepted dataset associations while protecting against co-alteration, lineage-specific, and batch-driven artifacts. For NFE2L2, the accepted reversed KEAP1-loss finding is very large, so I registered two specificity audits: whether the KEAP1-loss effect differs between adenocarcinoma and non-adenocarcinoma lineage subtypes, and whether it differs in STK11-loss versus STK11-intact cells. I also registered STK11 loss itself against NFE2L2 dependency as a co-alteration control; if STK11 loss shows a large effect, the KEAP1 association may be less specific and could reflect co-occurring alterations. For the accepted SMARCA2 associations, I registered batch-heterogeneity checks and conditional specificity analyses: the SMARCA4-loss effect in ARID1A-intact cells, the ARID1A-loss effect in SMARCA4-intact cells, and an interaction between SMARCA4 loss and batch_a. These test whether the SWI/SNF paralog signal is concentrated in particular genetic or technical contexts. For the accepted and validated TP53-loss/USP7 association, I registered a batch_a interaction audit because the effect is unusually large; if it is robust, the interaction estimate should be close to zero. For unresolved borderline associations, I registered lineage-interaction tests for KRAS-dependency and MDM2-dependency effects rather than only repeating subgroup mean differences, because interaction estimates directly test whether adenocarcinoma status modifies the predictor effect. I avoided interaction subgroup tests for very rare exposed groups, such as MSI-high in non-adenocarcinoma or small amplification subsets where comparison cells may not satisfy the 20-observation rule. As before, these remain association hypotheses in the supplied dataset, not causal or externally generalizable claims. All estimates are interpreted in the signed direction of each registered claim.

I selected 12 previously registered, currently untested comparisons that best advance the run: robustness and specificity checks for the four largest accepted dataset associations, plus follow-up of two borderline oncogene-dependency effects. For the accepted KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 association, I ran the batch-a interaction audit, adenocarcinoma interaction audit, STK11 interaction audit, and STK11-loss main effect. These test whether the very large reversed KEAP1-loss effect is technically batch-driven, lineage-specific, or confounded by co-occurring STK11 loss. For SMARCA2, I ran a batch-a interaction audit for SMARCA4 loss, a conditional SMARCA4-loss effect in ARID1A-intact cells, and a conditional ARID1A-loss effect in SMARCA4-intact cells; together these assess whether the SMARCA4/SMARCA2 signal is context-specific and whether the negative overall ARID1A signal hides any SMARCA4-intact effect. For USP7, I ran a batch-a interaction audit and an adenocarcinoma subgroup effect to check whether the validated TP53-loss/USP7 association is stable across batch and lineage context. For WRN, I ran the adenocarcinoma subgroup effect to determine whether the MSI-high/WRN synthetic-lethality-like association is confined to adenocarcinoma or present broadly. Finally, I ran KRAS-dependency and EGFR-dependency effects in adenocarcinoma to resolve the borderline overall KRAS and EGFR results. I deferred MDM2 lineage follow-up and some broader interaction claims because the current selected set better prioritizes robustness of accepted large effects and the two most informative unresolved borderline effects. All estimates will be interpreted as already signed to the registered hypothesis direction: positive values support the registered direction, negative values oppose it. I will judge clinical relevance using a 10% relative difference against each outcome's baseline mean scale, and conclusions remain limited to associations in this supplied dataset rather than causal or generalizable claims.

I assessed all newly delivered estimates as already signed to the registered hypothesis direction. A positive signed estimate supports the registered direction, and a negative signed estimate opposes it. For clinically meaningful magnitude, I used a 10% relative-difference threshold on the absolute overall mean of each dependency outcome. KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 robustness: H23 batch_a interaction estimate +0.021, interval -0.031 to +0.072. This is smaller than the main effect of about +0.796 and uncertain, so it neither demonstrates positive batch_a amplification nor excludes it; I leave it unresolved and deferred. H26 lineage interaction estimate -0.012, interval -0.057 to +0.033, and H27 STK11-loss interaction estimate -0.026, interval -0.079 to +0.026, also show no robust positive interaction and are small relative to the KEAP1 main effect. H28 STK11-loss main effect on NFE2L2 estimate -0.007, below the NFE2L2 threshold and interval-crossing, provides a useful specificity control against a simple STK11-confounding explanation. Taken together, these audits do not strongly undermine H18, so I request independent validation of H18. SMARCA2/SMARCA4: H29 batch_a interaction is statistically and practically meaningful but opposite to the registered direction: signed estimate -0.051, interval -0.095 to -0.007, beyond the SMARCA2 threshold of about 0.0415. This suggests that the SMARCA4-loss effect on SMARCA2 dependency is attenuated in batch_a, not absent overall. I reject H29 as stated but register a reversed interaction claim and a batch_a-specific mean-effect follow-up. H33 ARID1A-loss effect in SMARCA4-intact cells is small and interval-crossing, so it is rejected and closed. H34 SMARCA4-loss effect in ARID1A-intact cells is enormous and precise, supporting the specificity of the SMARCA4/SMARCA2 paralog signal and strengthening confidence in H7 pending validation. USP7/TP53: H25 adenocarcinoma effect is large and precise, +0.799, interval +0.776 to +0.823, supporting the validated TP53-loss/USP7 association in the dominant lineage. H30 batch_a interaction is negative and uncertain; it does not evidence positive batch_a amplification, so I leave it unresolved but deferred because H12 is already validated. WRN/MSI-high: H24 adenocarcinoma effect is large and precise, +0.784, interval +0.748 to +0.820, supporting H13. KRAS and EGFR adenocarcinoma refinements: H19 estimate +0.0115 and H20 estimate +0.0198, both below their respective 10% outcome thresholds and interval-crossing, including threshold-level possibilities. These remain unresolved and deferred because neither the overall nor the adenocarcinoma effects provide clinically compelling evidence. All conclusions remain dataset associations, not causal or externally generalizable claims.

I reassessed the due validation for H18. The estimate is already signed to the hypothesis direction, so the discovery signed estimate of about +0.796 and validation signed estimate of about +0.781 both support the registered direction: KEAP1-loss cells have a less negative NFE2L2 dependency score, i.e. weaker NFE2L2 dependency. The independent validation interval is multiplicity-aware and remains entirely positive, approximately +0.752 to +0.809. Using the absolute overall NFE2L2 mean of about 0.093 as the baseline scale, the 10% clinical-significance threshold is about 0.0093; the validation effect is far above that threshold. Therefore the overall H18 association is well supported in this supplied dataset and I close the original overall investigation. This result also reinforces rejection of the original H5 direction: the data do not support KEAP1 loss causing stronger NFE2L2 dependency; instead the opposite association is supported. The earlier specificity audits did not show a strong batch_a, adenocarcinoma, or STK11-loss interaction, and STK11 loss alone was null-like for NFE2L2, so the validation now makes this one of the two strongest validated in-dataset findings, alongside validated TP53-loss/USP7. These remain associations within the supplied dataset, not causal statements or claims about external generalizability. Next, I propose two conditional KEAP1-loss analyses: within TP53-loss cells and within STK11-loss cells, to test whether the very large KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 association persists in important co-alteration contexts. I also propose a WRN-by-adenocarcinoma interaction to test whether MSI-high/WRN dependency is lineage-subtype-specific. If future analyses do not undermine the major accepted effects, the next validation priority should be one of the strongest unvalidated accepted overall associations, preferably SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 or MSI-high/WRN.

I registered follow-up comparisons that address three complementary questions: whether the large accepted dataset associations persist in important co-alteration and technical contexts, whether lineage or driver context modifies the accepted dependencies, and whether the borderline KRAS and EGFR effects become clinically meaningful in biologically defined subsets. For KEAP1 loss and NFE2L2 dependency, the accepted direction is weaker NFE2L2 dependency, registered as positive signed effects; therefore the new conditional claims test whether this association persists among TP53-intact, KRAS-mutant, and EGFR-amplified cells. If the signed effects remain large and positive, the KEAP1/NFE2L2 finding is robust across driver contexts; if absent or much smaller in a context, the overall association may be co-alteration driven or context-specific. For TP53 loss and USP7 dependency, the validated accepted direction is weaker USP7 dependency, so I tested the association among KEAP1-loss cells and in batch_a. These audits address co-alteration and technical heterogeneity. For SMARCA4 loss and stronger SMARCA2 dependency, I proposed adenocarcinoma, ARID1A-loss, and non-Avana library conditional means. The adenocarcinoma context is biologically and numerically informative; ARID1A-loss context tests whether the SMARCA4 effect remains large when a related SWI/SNF component is also lost, complementing the ARID1A-intact specificity result; the non-Avana context checks whether the large association is an Avana-library artifact. For WRN and MSI-high, the accepted direction is stronger WRN dependency; I tested the association among higher mutation-burden samples to assess whether MSI-high status and mutation burden convey overlapping biological information. For KRAS and EGFR dependency, the overall effects have been unresolved and below or near the 10% relative threshold. I therefore registered driver-context tests: KRAS-mutation effect among TP53-intact cells and EGFR-amplification effect among KRAS-wildtype cells. These contexts are common enough for the comparison-cell rule and could reveal a subgroup where the association crosses the clinical-significance threshold. If these conditional estimates remain small or interval-crossing, the simplest conclusion is that these predictors do not have scientifically meaningful differences in dependency within this dataset. These are associations in the supplied data, not causal or externally generalizable claims.

I selected twelve currently untested comparisons that most directly test the robustness, specificity, and biological generality of the strongest accepted in-dataset associations, while also targeting the two unresolved borderline oncogene-dependency effects. For SMARCA4 loss and stronger SMARCA2 dependency, I ran batch_a-specific mean effect H36, adenocarcinoma-restricted effect H45, ARID1A-loss co-alteration context H46, and non-Avana library context H47. These test whether the large SMARCA4/SMARCA2 signal is technically or genetically context-specific rather than a broad dataset association. For the validated KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 association, I ran H37 and H38, which ask whether the effect persists among TP53-loss and STK11-loss cells. These are important co-alteration contexts; if the effect remains large and positive there, the association is less likely to be an artifact of a simple co-mutation pattern. For the validated TP53-loss/USP7 association, I ran H43 and H44, which test whether it persists among KEAP1-loss cells and within batch_a. These address co-alteration and batch heterogeneity. For MSI-high and stronger WRN dependency, I ran H39 and H48 to assess lineage-subtype modification and whether the effect persists in higher mutation-burden cells, a relevant potential confounder because MSI-high samples often have elevated mutation burden. Finally, I ran H49 and H50 to test whether the borderline KRAS-mutation/KRAS-dependency and EGFR-amplification/EGFR-dependency effects become meaningful in driver-relevant subsets: TP53-intact cells for KRAS and KRAS-wildtype cells for EGFR. If these remain small or interval-crossing, the simplest conclusion is that no clinically meaningful difference is supported in this dataset for those predictors. All returned estimates should be interpreted as already signed to the registered hypothesis direction: positive values support the registered direction, negative values oppose it. I will judge practical importance against a 10% relative threshold using the absolute overall mean of each dependency outcome. These comparisons remain associations within the supplied dataset, not causal or externally generalizable claims.

All returned estimates are interpreted as already signed to the registered hypothesis direction, so positive signed estimates support the registered claim and negative signed estimates oppose it. For practical importance, I used a 10% relative threshold against the absolute overall mean of each dependency outcome: SMARCA2 about 0.0415, NFE2L2 about 0.0093, USP7 about 0.0093, WRN about 0.0301, KRAS about 0.0245, and EGFR about 0.0250. The new conditional results strongly reinforce the major accepted associations. H36 shows a very large positive signed SMARCA4-loss effect on SMARCA2 dependency within batch_a: +0.747, interval +0.709 to +0.785. Although somewhat smaller than the overall estimate, it is far above the SMARCA2 threshold and entirely positive, so the SMARCA4/SMARCA2 association is not absent in batch_a. H45, H46, and H47 similarly show large positive effects in adenocarcinoma, ARID1A-loss cells, and non-Avana libraries: +0.777, +0.814, and +0.801, respectively, all with intervals well above the practical threshold. Together these substantially strengthen H7 and support requesting independent validation of H7. H37 and H38 show that the KEAP1-loss/weak NFE2L2 association persists in TP53-loss and STK11-loss co-alteration contexts: +0.810 and +0.775, both precise and enormous relative to the NFE2L2 threshold. This makes a simple co-mutation-confounding explanation for H18 less plausible. H43 and H44 show that the validated TP53-loss/USP7 association persists among KEAP1-loss cells and within batch_a: +0.794 and +0.789, both large and precise. H48 shows that MSI-high cells have stronger WRN dependency among higher-mutation-burden samples: +0.780, interval +0.749 to +0.811, well above the WRN threshold. This supports H13 and argues against the idea that the MSI-high/WRN association is merely an artifact of very low mutation-burden cases. H39 is the WRN adenocarcinoma interaction: signed estimate -0.021, interval -0.085 to +0.042. This does not support a positive lineage-subtype-specific interaction and is not practically meaningful at the point estimate; however, the interval is wide enough to leave the interaction formally unresolved. Because the overall and adenocarcinoma-specific WRN effects are already strong, I close this interaction investigation without treating it as evidence against the main WRN association. The borderline KRAS and EGFR follow-ups remain unsupported as clinically meaningful effects. H49 gives a TP53-intact KRAS-mutation signed effect of +0.0166, interval -0.0031 to +0.0363, below the KRAS threshold and interval-crossing. H50 gives a KRAS-wildtype EGFR-amplification signed effect of +0.0162, interval -0.0135 to +0.0459, below the EGFR threshold and interval-crossing. With these conditional checks now small and nonsignificant, I close further subgroup investigation for these two predictors, but I keep them unresolved rather than rejecting them because the confidence intervals remain compatible with small-to-moderate positive effects and do not cleanly exclude the clinical threshold. Overall, the new evidence favors validation of the SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 association, reinforces the KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 and TP53-loss/USP7 associations, and supports the MSI-high/WRN association, while leaving the borderline KRAS and EGFR dependency effects scientifically weak in this supplied dataset. These remain in-dataset associations, not causal or externally generalizable claims.

The newly delivered independent validation strongly confirms the two major accepted associations and a key subgroup validation. All estimates are already signed to the registered hypothesis direction. For H12, TP53 loss/USP7 dependency, the validation signed estimate is +0.797 with an independent interval of approximately +0.769 to +0.824. Against the absolute overall USP7 mean of about 0.093, the 10% practical threshold is about 0.0093, so the validated association is overwhelmingly above that threshold and entirely positive. This supports weaker USP7 dependency in TP53-loss cells and confirms the discovery effect; I accept and close H12. For H7, SMARCA4 loss/SMARCA2 dependency, the validation signed estimate is +0.807 with interval approximately +0.777 to +0.838. The practical threshold for SMARCA2 is about 0.0415; the interval is far above that level. Combined with the precise discovery estimate and the supportive conditional analyses in batch_a, adenocarcinoma, ARID1A-loss, and non-Avana contexts, this validates that SMARCA4-loss cells have much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, i.e. a much more negative SMARCA2 score. I accept and close H7. The accepted H35 batch_a interaction remains meaningful as a context effect: the SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 dependency effect is attenuated in batch_a relative to its complement, but the main effect is so large and now independently validated that further pursuit of this technical interaction is not the most informative next step. I close H35. For H24, MSI-high/WRN dependency within adenocarcinoma, the validation signed estimate is +0.784 with interval approximately +0.727 to +0.840. The WRN practical threshold is about 0.0301, so this subgroup effect is also overwhelmingly above the clinical threshold and fully supported. This validates the adenocarcinoma-specific MSI-high/WRN association and reinforces H13. I accept and close H24. H13 remains accepted as an overall in-dataset association because the discovery overall effect is very large and precise, and it is further supported by the adenocarcinoma validation and by the higher-mutation-burden subset effect. I keep H13 active rather than closing it only because independent validation of the overall MSI-high/WRN effect would be a valuable way to distinguish robust in-dataset association from subgroup or discovery-set stability; if validation capacity permits, it is a high-value next request. The validated accepted findings are therefore SMARCA4 loss/stronger SMARCA2 dependency, KEAP1 loss/weaker NFE2L2 dependency, TP53 loss/weaker USP7 dependency, and MSI-high/stronger WRN dependency in adenocarcinoma, with overall MSI-high/WRN supported but not yet overall-independent validated. These are dataset associations, not causal statements or claims of external generalizability. Negative or weak evidence remains for BRFAF V600E/BRAF dependency, ERBB2 amplification/ERBB2 dependency, MYC amplification/POLR2A dependency, ARID1A loss/SMARCA2 dependency without SMARCA4 loss, STK11 loss/NFE2L2 dependency, and RB1 loss/KIF18A dependency. The KRAS mutation/KRAS dependency and EGFR amplification/EGFR dependency effects remain scientifically borderline: multiple overall, lineage, and driver-context checks have point estimates near but generally below the 10% threshold or with intervals crossing zero and threshold, so I do not accept them as clinically meaningful associations in this supplied dataset. Next, I registered focused follow-ups: EGFR amplification among TP53-intact cells and KRAS mutation among EGFR-wildtype cells to test whether borderline oncogene effects become meaningful in mutually relevant driver backgrounds; MSI-high/WRN among lower mutation-burden samples to test independence from high mutation burden; KEAP1 loss/NFE2L2 among EGFR-wildtype cells as another co-alteration robustness check; and EGFR amplification/STAT3 dependency as a pathway-level cross-talk hypothesis. These comparisons remain in-dataset exploratory tests of association and specificity.

I registered comparisons for three scientific purposes: (1) to test whether the large accepted associations are robust within the dominant lineage subtype and whether subtype modifies them, (2) to test whether co-alterations modify the accepted associations beyond the conditional means already examined, and (3) to probe biologically plausible but still untested synthetic-lethal or signaling-bypass relationships. For accepted effects, signed estimates will be interpreted against the registered direction: SMARCA4 loss is expected to give a more negative SMARCA2 score, i.e. stronger SMARCA2 dependency, so the main and interaction hypotheses are registered with direction -1; TP53 loss and KEAP1 loss are expected to give less negative USP7 and NFE2L2 scores, i.e. weaker dependency, so those hypotheses are registered with direction +1. The adenocarcinoma mean for KEAP1 loss/NFE2L2 asks whether the validated overall weak-NFE2L2 association is also directly supported in the largest lineage subtype. The lineage-subtype interactions for SMARCA4/SMARCA2 and TP53/USP7 compare adenocarcinoma with its complement in the same eligible population; a near-zero estimate would argue against strong subtype modification, while a sizeable signed estimate would indicate that the accepted effect is concentrated or attenuated by subtype. The KEAP1-by-TP53-loss and KEAP1-by-KRAS-mutation interactions quantify whether these co-alteration contexts change the size of the KEAP1/NFE2L2 association, not merely whether the effect is present in each context. For TP53 loss/RPL11, I expect TP53-loss cells to show weaker RPL11 dependency because RPL11 participates in the p53-MDM2 regulatory axis, so the signed direction is +1; alternatives are no association or a compensatory stronger dependency. For DNA repair and replication stress, I registered BRCA2-loss associations with WRN and DHX9, expecting stronger dependency (more negative scores, direction -1) because BRCA2 deficiency may increase reliance on helicases that maintain replication-fork and R-loop/G-quadruplex homeostasis. The BRCA2-loss effect on WRN among MSI-intact cells and the MSI-high effect on WRN among BRCA2-intact cells test whether these DNA-repair associations are independent rather than mutually confounded. For signaling bypass, I tested PIK3CA mutation/EGFR among EGFR-amplification-intact cells and NF1 loss/KRAS among KRAS-wildtype cells. In both cases I expect a positive raw contrast, i.e. weaker dependency on the upstream receptor or RAS pathway gene, because downstream pathway activation can bypass the measured exposure; null or opposite effects are scientifically plausible alternatives. For practical importance, I will compare signed estimates with approximate 10% thresholds based on the absolute overall means: WRN about 0.030, DHX9 about 0.025, RPL11 about 0.025, EGFR about 0.025, KRAS about 0.025, NFE2L2 about 0.0093, USP7 about 0.0093, and SMARCA2 about 0.042. All proposed comparisons remain tests of association in the supplied dataset, not causal claims or claims of external generalizability.

I selected twelve untested comparisons that jointly address three high-value questions: (1) whether the already accepted large associations are stable in the dominant adenocarcinoma subtype and are modified by biologically relevant co-alterations; (2) whether TP53 loss has additional pathway-consistent dependency associations beyond USP7 and MDM2; and (3) whether DNA-repair deficiency or downstream signaling bypass produces new, clinically meaningful associations. All returned estimates will be interpreted as already signed to the registered hypothesis direction, so positive signed values support the registered claim and negative values oppose it. For mean differences, I will judge practical importance using a 10% relative threshold based on the absolute overall mean: NFE2L2 and USP7 about 0.0093, SMARCA2 about 0.0415, RPL11 about 0.0252, WRN about 0.0301, DHX9 about 0.0250, EGFR about 0.0250, and KRAS about 0.0245. Interactions will be judged similarly for the size of context-specific modification, with near-zero estimates supporting no important modification. H56 directly tests the KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 association in adenocarcinoma, the largest subtype, strengthening or localizing the accepted overall effect. H57 and H58 test whether the SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 and TP53-loss/USP7 effects are concentrated or attenuated in adenocarcinoma relative to its complement. H59 and H60 quantify KEAP1-loss effects in TP53-loss and KRAS-mutant backgrounds relative to their complements, addressing whether co-alteration changes the magnitude rather than merely whether the association remains visible. H61 tests TP53 loss versus RPL11 dependency, a biologically coherent p53-pathway follow-up to the accepted USP7 result and the unresolved MDM2 result; a large positive signed effect would support weaker RPL11 dependency in TP53-loss cells and could merit validation. H62 through H65 test DNA-repair synthetic-lethality and independence hypotheses: BRCA2 loss with WRN and DHX9 dependency, with BRCA2 loss in MSI-intact cells and MSI-high dependency in BRCA2-intact cells separating overlapping replication-stress biology. H66 and H67 test signaling-bypass hypotheses: PIK3CA mutation among EGFR-amplification-intact cells and NF1 loss among KRAS-wildtype cells. For these bypass claims, a positive signed mean difference means weaker dependency on EGFR or KRAS, respectively, consistent with downstream pathway activation. If any of these new associations is large and precisely estimated, it should be considered for independent validation; otherwise the accepted associations remain the primary supported dataset findings. These analyses remain associations within the supplied data, not causal or externally generalizable claims.

All estimates are interpreted as already signed to the registered hypothesis direction, so positive signed estimates support the registered claim and negative signed estimates oppose it. I used approximate 10% practical thresholds from the absolute overall means: NFE2L2 and USP7 about 0.0093, SMARCA2 about 0.0415, WRN about 0.0301, RPL11 about 0.0252, DHX9 about 0.0250, EGFR about 0.0250, and KRAS about 0.0245. H56 is a direct adenocarcinoma-subtype test of the accepted KEAP1-loss association with weaker NFE2L2 dependency: +0.793, interval +0.769 to +0.817. This is overwhelmingly above the NFE2L2 practical threshold and highly precise, so I accept and close it. It reinforces H18 but does not imply causality or external generalizability. H57 and H58 test whether adenocarcinoma versus non-adenocarcinoma modifies the SMARCA4/SMARCA2 and TP53/USP7 effects. Their point estimates are small, intervals cross zero, and they are not decisive for clinically meaningful modification; they remain unresolved, but I close further pursuit because the main effects are already strong and independently validated. H59 and H60 test whether TP53 loss or KRAS mutation modifies the KEAP1/NFE2L2 association. Both have small positive point estimates with intervals crossing zero and compatible with meaningful modification, so I do not accept effect modification; I keep them unresolved and close further work because the main KEAP1 association is already validated and context-specific mean checks have repeatedly shown large effects. H61 tests TP53 loss versus RPL11 dependency. The point estimate +0.0037 is far below the RPL11 threshold, and the upper bound +0.0237 is slightly below the 10% practical threshold; thus there is no evidence of a clinically meaningful weaker RPL11 dependency in TP53-loss cells, so I reject and close. H62-H64 probe BRCA2-loss synthetic lethality with WRN and DHX9. The point estimates are essentially null or small; the intervals are wide enough to leave small-to-moderate effects formally unresolved, but the evidence does not support the registered associations. I keep them unresolved but close further work because there is no signal comparable to the accepted associations. H65 is important: MSI-high cells have much stronger WRN dependency among BRCA2-intact cells: +0.794, interval +0.764 to +0.825. This supports H13 independently of BRCA2-loss co-occurrence and is accepted and closed as a robust in-dataset context. H66, PIK3CA mutation among EGFR-amplification-intact cells, opposes the registered bypass direction and excludes a clinically meaningful positive effect; reject and close. H67 is the main new signal: NF1 loss among KRAS-wildtype cells is associated with weaker KRAS dependency: +0.0387, interval +0.0062 to +0.0712. The point estimate exceeds the KRAS 10% threshold and the interval excludes zero, making it biologically plausible and statistically positive, but the lower bound is below the practical threshold. Therefore I keep H67 unresolved and active rather than accept it; registered refinements will test whether the signal persists in TP53-intact, EGFR-amplification-intact, and adenocarcinoma contexts. I request validation for H13 because overall MSI-high/WRN is accepted and repeatedly supported, including by H65, but the overall effect itself has not yet received independent validation.

The new validation evidence confirms the two remaining high-value in-dataset associations. For H18, KEAP1 loss versus NFE2L2 dependency is registered in the direction of weaker NFE2L2 dependency; the independent validation signed estimate is +0.781, with interval +0.752 to +0.809. The 10% practical threshold for NFE2L2 is about 0.0093, so the validation interval is entirely and far above that threshold. Combined with the discovery estimate +0.796, this strongly supports KEAP1-loss cells having much weaker NFE2L2 dependency in this supplied dataset. I therefore accept and close H18. For H13, MSI-high versus WRN dependency is registered in the direction of stronger WRN dependency, i.e. a more negative WRN score. The newly delivered overall validation signed estimate is +0.771, interval +0.720 to +0.822. The WRN 10% threshold is about 0.0301, so the independent interval is also entirely and overwhelmingly above the practical threshold. This validates the overall MSI-high/WRN association, not only the adenocarcinoma subgroup result already validated in H24. I therefore accept and close H13. The core validated set is now SMARCA4 loss/stronger SMARCA2 dependency, TP53 loss/weaker USP7 dependency, KEAP1 loss/weaker NFE2L2 dependency, and MSI-high/stronger WRN dependency overall and in adenocarcinoma. The most informative unresolved signal is the NF1-loss bypass signal for KRAS dependency. The discovery result in KRAS-wildtype cells was +0.0387, interval +0.0062 to +0.0712, exceeding the KRAS threshold at the point estimate and excluding zero, but the lower bound is below the 10% practical threshold. I keep H67 unresolved and prioritize its registered context refinements plus two new analyses: a specificity interaction to test whether the NF1-loss effect is larger in KRAS-wildtype than KRAS-mutant cells, and a direct KRAS-mutation test in NF1-intact cells to see whether the borderline KRAS effect becomes meaningful when NF1-loss confounding is reduced. The borderline KRAS and EGFR main effects remain unresolved but are deferred rather than accepted; their existing intervals remain compatible with small effects crossing zero and threshold. The TP53-loss/MDM2 effect also remains unresolved but deferred, because the point estimate is small and the confidence interval only partly overlaps the practical threshold. These statements are associations within the supplied dataset and not claims of causality or external generalizability.

The accepted and independently validated core in-dataset associations remain: SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency; TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency; KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency; and MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency overall and in adenocarcinoma. The most actionable unresolved signal is the NF1-loss/bypass signal for KRAS dependency. The discovery mean difference among KRAS-wildtype cells was +0.0387, interval +0.0062 to +0.0712, signed toward weaker KRAS dependency. The point estimate exceeds the KRAS 10% practical threshold of about 0.0245 and excludes zero, but the confidence interval is still compatible with subthreshold effects. I therefore registered refinements that test whether the NF1-loss effect persists and is context-specific: whether it is modified by TP53 loss, adenocarcinoma subtype, or screen batch; and whether a direct KRAS-mutation effect becomes clearer when NF1-loss and TP53-loss contexts are removed. I also added a mechanistic pathway check asking whether NF1 loss is associated with weaker RIT1 dependency, a more upstream RAS-pathway gene, which would be consistent with pathway bypass but is not required. Next, I proposed refinements to borderline oncogene hypotheses. For BRAF and ERBB2, the overall tests were not accepted; conditional tests in mutually cleaner genetic contexts may reveal oncogene addiction effects that were diluted by co-alterations. For RIT1, KRAS mutation is expected to reduce dependency on upstream RAS-pathway input, so I registered a weaker-dependency direction. For STAT3, ERBB2 amplification is a plausible activator of STAT3 signaling, with stronger STAT3 dependency expected. For USP7, MYC amplification is a plausible test of deubiquitinase-dependency relationships, though alternative null or opposite directions remain possible. For DHX9, MSI-high is expected to show stronger helicase replication-stress dependency if the accepted WRN effect reflects broader replication stress, but the null is that WRN is the specific helicase dependency. These remain in-dataset association tests, not causal claims or claims of external generalizability.

I selected twelve active, previously untested comparisons that best address the current priorities: resolve the borderline NF1-loss/KRAS-dependency signal, assess whether direct KRAS-mutation effects are masked by co-alterations, revisit mutually cleaner oncogene contexts, and test biologically coherent pathway or replication-stress follow-ups. All returned estimates will be interpreted as already signed to the registered hypothesis direction; positive values support the registered claim and negative values oppose it. Practical mean-difference thresholds are approximately KRAS 0.0245, BRAF 0.0248, ERBB2 0.0260, RIT1 0.0256, STAT3 0.0282, DHX9 0.0250, and MDM2 0.0269, using 10% of the absolute overall outcome mean. H68-H70 test whether the NF1-loss association among KRAS-wildtype cells persists in TP53-intact, EGFR-amplification-intact, and adenocarcinoma contexts, where the registered direction +1 corresponds to weaker KRAS dependency. H71 is the key specificity interaction: with direction -1, a positive signed estimate means the NF1-loss effect is larger in KRAS-wildtype than in KRAS-mutant cells. H72 tests direct KRAS-mutation dependency among NF1-intact cells, assessing whether NF1-loss co-alteration dilutes the direct KRAS mutation effect. H83 tests pathway coherence by asking whether NF1 loss also predicts weaker RIT1 dependency among KRAS-wildtype cells. H77 and H78 revisit BRAF and ERBB2 oncogene dependencies in contexts where a common alternative driver is absent: KRAS-wildtype cells for BRAF and EGFR-amplification-intact cells for ERBB2. H79 and H80 test pathway dependencies: KRAS mutation versus RIT1 dependency and ERBB2 amplification versus STAT3 dependency. H82 tests whether MSI-high predicts stronger DHX9 dependency, a specificity check for the accepted MSI-high/WRN association. H21 resolves the unresolved TP53-loss/MDM2 pathway signal within the largest lineage subtype. These analyses are discovery association tests in the supplied dataset, not causal or external-generality claims.

All estimates below are already signed to the registered hypothesis direction, so positive values support the registered claim and negative values oppose it. I used approximate 10% practical thresholds from the absolute overall means: KRAS about 0.0245, BRAF about 0.0248, ERBB2 about 0.0260, RIT1 about 0.0256, STAT3 about 0.0282, DHX9 about 0.0250, and MDM2 about 0.0269. For the NF1-loss/KRAS-dependency signal, H68 is the strongest clean context so far: NF1 loss among KRAS-wildtype and TP53-intact cells has signed estimate +0.0428, interval +0.0048 to +0.0807, indicating weaker KRAS dependency. It excludes zero and exceeds the practical threshold at the point estimate, but the lower bound is still well below the 10% threshold, so it does not establish a clinically meaningful effect. H69 is similar but with lower bound only +0.0011, and H70 in adenocarcinoma crosses zero. H71 suggests context specificity, but the signed interaction +0.0674 has lower bound essentially at zero and relies on a small KRAS-mutant/NF1-loss cell with only 49 observations, so it is not decisive. H72 directly tests KRAS mutation among NF1-intact cells and is near null, +0.0076; it cannot establish a meaningful direct KRAS-dependency effect. H83 does not support coherent pathway bypass through RIT1, +0.0115. Overall, the NF1/KRAS results are biologically coherent and consistently positive in several contexts, but the discovery intervals are too imprecise to assert at least 10% weaker KRAS dependency. I therefore request independent validation for H67, the broader KRAS-wildtype NF1-loss context, because it is the primary unresolved claim and has slightly larger exposure cells than the TP53-intact refinement. If validation supports a precise effect above the KRAS practical threshold, I can accept; if it remains borderline or crosses zero, the NF1/KRAS signal should remain unresolved or be closed. H77 opposes the registered BRAF-dependency direction in KRAS-wildtype cells and the maximum clinically meaningful positive effect is below the BRAF threshold, so reject and close. H78 is essentially null for conditional ERBB2 amplification among EGFR-amplification-intact cells; because the upper bound is only marginally above threshold, I keep it formally unresolved but close further work because there is no meaningful signal to pursue. H79 rejects the KRAS-mutation/RIT1 association because the interval upper bound is below the RIT1 practical threshold. H80 is not decisive for ERBB2-amplification/STAT3: point estimate is below threshold, interval crosses zero but includes possible meaningful effects; I defer it as low priority. H82 does not support MSI-high/DHX9 as a parallel replication-stress dependency and I close it. H21 does not materially clarify TP53-loss/MDM2 in adenocarcinoma: point estimate remains below threshold and interval crosses zero; I defer it because the overall TP53-loss/MDM2 claim already remains borderline. These conclusions remain associations within the supplied dataset, not causal or externally generalizable claims.

Interpreting all estimates as already signed to the registered direction, the newly delivered validation evidence is decisive for the two response-deadline claims and largely closes the main NF1/KRAS frontier. H7, SMARCA4 loss versus stronger SMARCA2 dependency, is confirmed independently: validation signed estimate +0.807, interval +0.777 to +0.838. The practical 10 percent outcome threshold for SMARCA2 is about 0.0415, so the independent interval is far and uniformly above that threshold; combined with discovery, this is a robust in-dataset association and remains accepted and closed. H24, MSI-high versus stronger WRN dependency within adenocarcinoma, is also confirmed: validation signed estimate +0.784, interval +0.727 to +0.840, against a WRN threshold of about 0.0301. It is accepted and closed. The most important new result is H67, NF1 loss versus weaker KRAS dependency among KRAS-wildtype cells. Discovery was positive and excluded zero (+0.0387, +0.0062 to +0.0712), but the independent validation was essentially null (+0.0005, -0.0415 to +0.0425). The validation point estimate is far below the KRAS 10 percent practical threshold of about 0.0245 and provides no independent support for the broad claim. I therefore reject and close H67 as a general KRAS-wildtype association. This does not mathematically exclude a small or highly context-specific effect, but the broad signal discovered earlier is not supported by independent validation and should no longer be prioritized. The TP53-intact refinement H68 remains formally unresolved but deferred and low priority; the associated interaction and refinement claims H73 through H76 are closed. Supported findings in the supplied dataset are the large and repeatedly confirmed associations: SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency; TP53 loss is associated with much weaker USP7 dependency; KEAP1 loss is associated with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency; and MSI-high is associated with much stronger WRN dependency overall and in adenocarcinoma, with additional support in BRCA2-intact and higher mutation-burden contexts. Negative or unsupported findings include BRAF V600E not showing meaningful BRAF-dependency effects overall or in KRAS-wildtype cells, ERBB2 amplification not supporting meaningful ERBB2 dependency overall or in EGFR-amplification-intact cells, KRAS mutation not supporting weaker RIT1 dependency, TP53 loss not supporting meaningful RPL11 dependency, MSI-high not supporting DHX9 dependency, BRCA2-loss synthetic lethality patterns with WRN or DHX9 not supported, PIK3CA mutation not supporting bypass EGFR dependency, MYC amplification not supporting POLR2A dependency, and RB1 loss not supporting KIF18A dependency. Unresolved uncertainty remains for borderline effects such as EGFR amplification, KRAS mutation, TP53 loss with MDM2, ERBB2 amplification with STAT3, and residual NF1 contexts; these intervals cross zero or remain too imprecise relative to practical thresholds, and they are deferred or closed rather than accepted. The accepted batch interaction H35 should also be read cautiously because its lower confidence bound is well below the 10 percent SMARCA2 threshold despite the controller keeping it accepted. The most informative next analysis is H53, testing the MSI-high and WRN association in lower mutation-burden cells, because it interrogates robustness of one of the few large validated associations rather than chasing the failed NF1/KRAS signal. If further exploration is needed, broad untested predictors are higher yield than continued NF1/KRAS follow-up. All conclusions are associations within the supplied dataset, not claims of causality or external generalizability.

Core accepted associations remain robust in this supplied dataset: SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency; TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency; KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency; and MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency overall and in adenocarcinoma. The NF1-loss/KRAS-wildtype bypass signal failed independent validation, so I am deprioritizing further NF1/KRAS follow-up. The next round should test two complementary questions. First, technical specificity: do the accepted TP53-loss/USP7 and KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 effects persist outside the dominant Avana library? These are direct robustness checks against library-specific artifacts. Second, biologically coherent alternative predictors: CDKN2A loss may phenocopy aspects of p53 pathway loss through p14ARF loss, so I test weaker USP7 and weaker MDM2 dependency among TP53-intact cells. PTEN loss may bypass receptor or upstream RAS input through downstream PI3K/AKT activation, so I test weaker EGFR, KRAS-wildtype, and RIT1 dependency. BRAF V600E in KRAS-wildtype cells is another plausible bypass of upstream RIT1, while ERBB2 amplification may increase upstream input and strengthen RIT1 dependency. SMAD4 and STK11 loss are broadly untested pathway regulators with plausible STAT3-related effects. MYC amplification is tested against underexplored mitotic and secretory stress genes KIF18A and TMED10. For dependency scores, negative raw means stronger dependency; for bypass/less essentiality hypotheses, exposed-minus-comparator is positive and direction is +1. For stronger-dependency hypotheses, direction is -1. Practical 10% thresholds are roughly EGFR 0.0250, KRAS 0.0245, RIT1 0.0256, STAT3 0.0282, KIF18A 0.0256, TMED10 0.0253, USP7 0.0093, NFE2L2 0.0093, and MDM2 0.0269. These remain associations in the supplied dataset, not causal or external-generalizability claims.

I selected twelve untested active claims that best balance technical robustness, pathway coherence, and follow-up of accepted findings. H84 and H85 test whether the two largest validated pathway associations survive outside the dominant Avana library: KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency and TP53 loss with weaker USP7 dependency. These are specificity checks for library artifacts rather than new biological mechanisms. H86 and H87 ask whether CDKN2A loss in TP53-intact cells resembles aspects of p53-pathway loss for USP7 and MDM2 dependency. H88-H91 test a PI3K/RTK/RAS bypass family of hypotheses: PTEN loss as a downstream bypass of EGFR or KRAS-WT dependency, BRAF V600E as a bypass of RIT1 among KRAS-WT cells, and ERBB2 amplification as an upstream activator that could increase RIT1 dependency. H92 and H93 test broad STAT3 predictors, SMAD4 loss and STK11 loss. H94 tests a MYC association with the mitotic gene KIF18A. H53 is included instead of the more speculative MYC/TMED10 proposal because it directly interrogates the accepted MSI-high/WRN association in lower mutation-burden cells and can reveal whether the WRN effect is robust or mutation-burden dependent. All requested outputs will be interpreted as already signed to the registered direction: positive values support the registered claim, negative values oppose it. Practical 10 percent thresholds are roughly USP7 0.0093, NFE2L2 0.0093, MDM2 0.0269, EGFR 0.0250, KRAS 0.0245, RIT1 0.0256, STAT3 0.0282, KIF18A 0.0256, and WRN 0.0301. I will accept only when the direction and interval support an effect at or above the outcome-specific threshold; borderline intervals crossing zero or including subthreshold effects will remain unresolved or be closed if there is no informative signal. These remain associations in the supplied dataset, not causal or externally generalizable claims.

All estimates are already signed to the registered direction, so positive values support the registered hypothesis and negative values oppose it. I used practical 10% effect-size benchmarks from the absolute outcome means: NFE2L2 and USP7 about 0.0093, MDM2 about 0.0269, EGFR about 0.0250, KRAS about 0.0245, RIT1 about 0.0256, STAT3 about 0.0282, and KIF18A about 0.0256. H84 and H85 are decisive non-Avana robustness checks for the two core accepted associations. KEAP1 loss versus weaker NFE2L2 dependency among non-Avanna screens has signed estimate +0.794, interval +0.746 to +0.842; TP53 loss versus weaker USP7 dependency has +0.767, interval +0.703 to +0.832. These are far above the respective 10% thresholds and support the effects outside the dominant library, although they remain in-dataset associations. H86 does not support CDKN2A loss phenocopying TP53-loss-like weaker USP7 dependency among TP53-intact cells: point -0.0028, interval -0.0251 to +0.0195. The interval still includes small positive effects above the very small USP7 threshold, so I keep it formally unresolved but close further work as unpromising. H87 is not merely null; it strongly opposes the registered hypothesis that CDKN2A loss in TP53-intact cells gives weaker MDM2 dependency. Signed estimate -0.119, interval -0.158 to -0.079, indicating stronger MDM2 dependency. I reject the registered direction and close it, while proposing a new reversed claim because this opposite effect is clinically meaningful in magnitude. PTEN-loss bypass hypotheses are closed: H88 EGFR upper bound +0.0171 is below the EGFR threshold, and H89 KRAS-WT upper bound +0.0216 is below the KRAS threshold. H90 is the most interesting unresolved new result: BRAF V600E in KRAS-WT cells versus weaker RIT1 dependency has point +0.0128, interval -0.0213 to +0.0469. The upper bound exceeds the RIT1 10% threshold and the biological rationale is coherent, so I request validation. H91 ERBB2 amplification versus stronger RIT1 dependency is closed/rejected because the maximum signed positive effect +0.0230 is below the RIT1 threshold. H92, H93, and H94 have point estimates below their practical thresholds and are therefore not accepted; their intervals include possible meaningful positive effects, so I keep them unresolved but deferred as lower-priority broad predictor screens. H53 was invalid because the low mutation-burden MSI-high cell had zero observations; it is closed as infeasible rather than evidence against an effect. I also reassess H35: the batch interaction point estimate exceeds the SMARCA2 10% benchmark, but its lower bound +0.0069 is well below that benchmark, so accepting it as clinically meaningful is not justified without independent validation or a more precise interval; I change it to unresolved and deferred.

All estimates are interpreted as already signed to the registered hypothesis direction, so positive values support the registered claim and negative values oppose it. I used approximately 10% practical thresholds from the absolute outcome means, for example KRAS about 0.0245, RIT1 about 0.0256, WRN about 0.0301, MDM2 about 0.0269, USP7 about 0.0093, and NFE2L2 about 0.0093. H13 remains accepted: MSI-high is associated with much stronger WRN dependency overall, discovery +0.790, interval +0.760 to +0.819, and independent validation +0.771, interval +0.720 to +0.822, far above the WRN threshold. H90 is rejected and closed: BRAF V600E among KRAS-wildtype cells had only borderline discovery for weaker RIT1 dependency, discovery +0.013, interval -0.021 to +0.047, and independent validation was near null and on the opposite side of the registered direction, validation -0.007, interval -0.056 to +0.041; although the wide adjusted interval still includes possible positive effects, the independent estimate provides no support for a clinically meaningful weaker-RIT1 effect. H49 is rejected and closed: KRAS mutation among TP53-intact cells was near null on validation for stronger KRAS dependency, validation +0.001, interval -0.028 to +0.030, with a point estimate far below the KRAS 10% threshold and a lower bound below zero; discovery alone was also below threshold. I reassessed H96 as an accepted in-dataset association: CDKN2A loss among TP53-intact cells is associated with much stronger MDM2 dependency, signed discovery +0.119, interval +0.079 to +0.158, well above the MDM2 threshold. This reverses the original H87 hypothesis and is the most informative new finding, but it remains active pending independent validation or technical robustness checks. Overall supported findings in the supplied dataset include SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, independently validated; TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency, independently validated and supported outside the dominant Avana library; KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, independently validated and supported outside Avana; and MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency overall and in adenocarcinoma, with additional support in higher mutation-burden and BRCA2-intact contexts. Negative or unsupported findings include NF1-loss as a broad KRAS-wildtype bypass, because validation was null; BRAF V600E with meaningful BRAF dependency; KRAS mutation with stronger KRAS dependency in TP53-intact cells; BRAF V600E with weaker RIT1 dependency among KRAS-wildtype cells; ERBB2 amplification with meaningful ERBB2 or RIT1 dependency; KRAS mutation with weaker RIT1 dependency; PTEN loss with EGFR or KRAS-wildtype bypass; PIK3CA mutation with EGFR bypass; MSI-high with DHX9 dependency; BRCA2-loss synthetic-lethality patterns for WRN or DHX9; MYC amplification with POLR2A dependency; RB1 loss with KIF18A dependency; TP53 loss with RPL11 dependency; and STK11 loss with NFE2L2 dependency overall. Unresolved uncertainty remains for borderline claims such as EGFR amplification, broad KRAS mutation, TP53 loss with MDM2, ERBB2 amplification with STAT3, several broad STAT3 and MYC predictors, and the SMARCA4 batch interaction H35, where the lower confidence bound remains below the practical 10% benchmark. The most informative next analysis is independent validation or technical and subgroup robustness of H96, CDKN2A loss in TP53-intact cells with stronger MDM2 dependency, including the proposed non-Avana and adenocarcinoma checks. Additional useful follow-up is the proposed conditional STK11-loss test among KEAP1-intact cells for NFE2L2 and the PIK3CA-mutation test among KRAS-wildtype cells. All conclusions are associations within the supplied dataset, not causal claims or claims of external generalizability.
